prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: [adversarial] Rowspan taller than its rows (language en).
Grid: 3 columns × 4 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Merged cells: "All three steps share on" spans 1 col × 3 row.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Step" · longest unbreakable word 35px · one-line width 35px
  col 2: header "Owner" · longest unbreakable word 48px · one-line width 48px
  col 3: header "Notes" · longest unbreakable word 76px · one-line width 1797px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Your understanding so far: {"purpose":"Show the owners of three sequential steps alongside a note shared by all three.","reading":"Readers scan down the steps and owners, then read the shared note as context for the whole sequence; its height spans all three rows.","groups":["Step and Owner form the row-by-row identification pair.","Notes applies to all three steps and carries the long-form context."],"keep_intact":["Step names and owner names","Individual words in the shared note"],"may_wrap":["The shared note can wrap naturally across lines; its merged cell can use the combined height of the three step rows."]}

The first image is the one-line content overview. The other images are real browser renders of your current designs:
Design r1A: widths [60, 75, 224] · table 360×283px · row heights [36, 82, 82, 82] · column headers wrapped 0/3 · tallest cell 10 lines · mid-word splits 0

Look carefully at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design say what works and what is visually wrong, and WHY it happens (which width causes it). Then propose up to 3 improved designs: refine the most promising, fix the problems you saw, and try a new idea if an important alternative is unexplored. If no design can be meaningfully improved, set "done": true and return no new designs.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"done":false,"designs":[{"name":"short-name","widths":[int px],"change":"what you changed and why"}]}

log.raw: {"critique":[{"design":"r1A","good":"The headers, step names, and owners remain intact. The three equal, tall rows make the sequence feel sparse, although the note remains readable.","cause":"The 224px Notes column gives the text 203px of usable width, producing ten lines. The merged cell's height is distributed across the three rows. This may reduce a line while retaining clear row labels and headers."},{"name":"balanced","widths":[58,72,229],"change":"Give Notes a modest increase while preserving a little more breathing room around the step and owner labels."},{"name":"compact-pair","widths":[57,69,233],"change":"Keep Owner at its minimum width for the header and give Step one extra pixel, testing a slightly different balance within the identification pair while retaining maximum space for the note."}]}
